summary: Specifies an extension to IEEE 802.11 for opportunistic, unauthenticated encryption of wireless traffic.

plainLanguage.summary: Encrypts open Wi-Fi so eavesdroppers cannot read it, without a password.

subtitle: Encrypting open Wi-Fi with a Diffie-Hellman exchange, so nobody needs a password.

tldr.problem: Open Wi-Fi networks send traffic unencrypted, and the common fix of a public shared passphrase does not actually stop a passive attacker, who knows the passphrase too.
tldr.mechanism: The client and access point run a Diffie-Hellman key exchange during 802.11 association, derive a Pairwise Master Key from it, and use that in the normal 4-way handshake instead of a PSK.
tldr.outcome: Traffic is encrypted without any configuration, but there is no authentication, so an active attacker impersonating the access point still wins. RFC 9672 updates this document.

today: RFC 8110 is an Informational document that has been updated by RFC 9672; it has not been obsoleted. It specifies encryption only, with no authentication.

sections.title: The Problem With Open and Public-PSK Wi-Fi
sections.content:
Coffee shops, airports and hotels commonly offer Internet access over Open (unencrypted) wireless, because distributing a passphrase or other authentication is not convenient. Traffic is then exposed to sniffing. Some venues instead print a shared, public Pre-Shared Key (PSK) on a sandwich board or menu, used in the 802.11 4-way handshake.

The RFC calls the belief that this protects users erroneous. Since everyone knows the PSK, a passive attacker who observes the 4-way handshake can compute the traffic encryption keys. If the attacker is too late, a forged deauthenticate frame makes the client and AP go through the handshake again.

Opportunistic Wireless Encryption (OWE) is a mode of opportunistic security (RFC 7435) for IEEE 802.11 that gives encryption but no authentication. It needs no special configuration or user interaction.
sections.plainLanguage: A password written on a chalkboard is no secret, because everyone who reads it can listen in. OWE makes a fresh secret for each visitor instead.

sections.title: The Diffie-Hellman Exchange
sections.content:
802.11 network access has two steps: 802.11 authentication (usually an empty exchange called Open Authentication) and then 802.11 association. OWE performs a Diffie-Hellman exchange at this point and feeds the result into the 4-way handshake in place of a PSK.

OWE uses a registry (the IANA IKE Diffie-Hellman group registry) that maps an integer to a full domain parameter set, and supports both elliptic curve (ECC) and finite field (FFC) groups. The hash algorithm depends on the group: for ECC, SHA-256 when the prime length is at most 256 bits, SHA-384 up to 384 bits, and SHA-512 above that. For FFC the cut-offs are 2048 and 3072 bits.

For interoperability a compliant implementation MUST support group 19, a 256-bit elliptic curve group.
sections.plainLanguage: Two people each mix a private colour into a shared paint tub and swap the results. Each can end up with the same final colour, but someone who only watches the swap cannot make it.

sections.title: Discovery and Association
sections.content:
An AP advertises OWE with an Authentication and Key Management (AKM) suite selector in the RSN element of every beacon and probe response. The suite is OUI 00-0F-AC, suite type 18. A client then does Open System authentication and proceeds to association.

OWE adds a Diffie-Hellman Parameter element (Element ID 255, Element ID Extension 32) to association requests and responses. It carries a two-octet group number in little-endian order followed by the public key. The client MUST indicate the OWE AKM and include the element in its request; the AP MUST include the OWE AKM in its response and, unless PMK caching is used, the element too.

If the AP does not support the requested group, it MUST answer with status code 77 (unsupported finite cyclic group). The client SHOULD retry with a different supported group. Invalid received keys MUST cause association to fail and the 802.11 state machine to reset. For FFC the check is 1 < element < p-1.
sections.plainLanguage: The access point puts up a sign saying it speaks the secret-code language. Each side hands over half of the code puzzle when they say hello, and if the code type is not understood, the client tries another.

sections.title: Keys After Association and PMK Caching
sections.content:
After association both sides compute z = F(DH(x, Y)), then prk = HKDF-extract(C | A | group, z) and PMK = HKDF-expand(prk, "OWE Key Generation", n), using the HKDF of RFC 5869. Here C and A are the client's and AP's public keys, and n is the bit length of the hash digest. The values z and prk SHOULD be irretrievably deleted once the PMK exists.

The PMKID is the leftmost 128 bits of the hash of C and A. The AP then starts the normal 4-way handshake with this PMK. The hash chosen earlier sets the integrity algorithm and key lengths (for example SHA-256 goes with HMAC-SHA-256 and a 128-bit KCK and KEK), and the result is keys for unicast and broadcast data.

PMK caching lets a client include a PMKID in its association request. If the AP has that PMK it returns the PMKID without a Diffie-Hellman Parameter element; otherwise it ignores the PMKID and does a normal OWE association.
sections.plainLanguage: The shared secret from the colour mixing is stirred into a strong set of keys. If you come back later, the access point can recognise your old keys and skip the mixing.

sections.title: Security Limits and Deployment Advice
sections.content:
OWE gives no authentication: the client has no authenticated identity for the AP and vice versa. The peers do share traffic keys and can be sure a frame from the peer was not modified in flight. OWE secures only the wireless hop, so users should still use application-level security end to end.

It is susceptible to an active attack in which an adversary impersonates an AP, induces a client to connect via OWE and connects to the real AP, letting it inspect, modify and forge data. OWE is not a replacement for any 802.11 authentication protocol and is not meant for use where real authentication is available.

On the deployment side, OWE is a replacement for Open authentication, so user interfaces should not show a lock icon for it. When replacing an existing Open or public-PSK network, an additional BSSID or a new ESS with a separate SSID is needed until most users have switched.
sections.plainLanguage: OWE stops people from overhearing, but it cannot tell you who you are whispering to. A fake access point can still trick you.

fields.desc: Variable-length octet string holding the Diffie-Hellman public key (width not to scale).
